A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same h4rm3l research. Their complete main texts and appendices support comparison, with algorithms, tables and figures traceable across the revised title and organization.

before.justification: v2 reports original attack-synthesis experiments, six-model safety benchmarks, human validation of its classifier, and defense experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical experiments and reports redesigned classifier validation, human-comparison results and synthesis timing measurements.

M1.justification: The compositional DSL, bandit selection rules, proposal-generation and pool-update procedures, and classifier prompt are retained. Expanded primitive and compiler documentation does not establish a changed algorithm or newly introduced method component.

E1.justification: Classifier validation expands from Claude-3-Haiku responses to responses from all six target LLMs, broadening the population tested for this task. The AdvBench attack evaluation and the datasets and model coverage of the defense experiments remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Section 3.3 and new Figure 11 evaluate human annotators against consensus labels alongside the automated classifier, adding an explicit human-performance comparator. The evaluated attack baselines, synthesis-method comparators and defense methods are retained; newly discussed related work is not added to those comparisons.

E3.justification: Classifier validation is substantially redesigned: v2 uses two authors labeling 100 Haiku responses and retains 93 agreed labels; v3 uses 576 annotations from seven humans on 122 responses sampled from a 360-response pool balanced across models and classes, with consensus labels excluding ties. The main synthesis settings and 50-prompt safety-benchmark protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds class-wise classifier and human error diagnostics with confusion matrices, plus synthesis runtime profiling in Appendices N and L. It also replaces the illustrative Haiku case with a Sonnet case. The existing abstraction ablation, attack-diversity analyses and defense studies are retained.

E5.justification: v2 reports classifier precision and recall with variability over three runs; v3 replaces these with point estimates without corresponding repeated-run or uncertainty information. Figure 6's standard errors and Appendix G's two-standard-deviation intervals are retained.

E6.justification: The redesigned validation replaces BAD BOT precision/recall of 88.3 ± 2.1% and 100 ± 0% with 72% and 76%, and adds 78% classifier accuracy, 93% human accuracy and detailed confusion results. These are different validation settings, not evidence of a same-setting performance decline. Table 5 adds synthesis durations of 25.14–33.63 hours; Tables 1–4 and the retained quantitative plots preserve their results.

T1.justification: Algorithm 1 newly states complexity O(Niters × Nproposals × killicit), and the ASR definition explicitly includes the original request as an argument to the harmfulness function. The Beta-distribution formulas are unchanged, and the decorator-composition equation is relocated to Appendix M; no substantial new proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The introduction expands the reported dataset contribution from 2,656 successful attacks to 15,891 attacks including that successful subset, and raises its highlighted synthesis-success claim from over 80% to over 90% ASR. The central contributions of compositional representation, bandit synthesis and safety benchmarking remain.

C2.justification: Section 6 recasts the importance of primitive names as a hypothesis, adds hyperparameter tradeoffs and guidance on validating classifiers under custom moderation policies, and removes the suggestion to use the classifier as a post-processing defense. The Anthropic account-filter limitation and principal transferability interpretations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix B substantially expands and revises primitive interfaces and initial-attack descriptions, with configuration-file locations. Appendix M adds compiler, base-class and generic-decorator code and defaults; Appendix L adds iteration counts and elapsed times. These materially expand reproducibility information, beyond the existing method explanation relocated into Appendix K.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion of LLM-Fuzzer, EasyJailbreak, disguise-and-reconstruction attacks and research on human jailbreakers, including an explicit comparison with template-based search. CodeBERT and Anthropic policy citations are also added. The central positioning around formal compositional attack synthesis is retained.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are substantially rewritten, method exposition is reorganized, benchmarking receives Section 3.4, and transferability discussion moves into the qualitative analysis. The Discussion and Appendix B are extensively restructured, producing substantial narrative changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The conference layout substantially reorganizes presentation: the retained benchmark heatmap moves from Figure 4 to the first page as Figure 1, the motivating attack illustration is replaced, and Figure 11 and Table 5 are added. Table captions are repositioned and expanded, while most existing quantitative graphics retain their content despite relocation or renumbering.

improvement.justification: Validation across all six models, explicit confusion matrices and substantially fuller implementation documentation improve scrutiny and reproducibility of the retained work. The gain is tempered by the removal of repeated-run uncertainty and the continued strong-alignment claim despite the new classifier's 72% BAD BOT precision and 76% recall. These changes support a limited overall improvement.
